newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark, Russia, sign Arctic fisheries deal.
newsitem.headline: Denmark, Russia, sign Arctic fisheries deal.

text.p: Danish and Russian firms joined forces on Thursday in a joint venture to increase Russian fishery production in the Barents Sea and give a welcome boost to Denmark's ailing shipbuilding industry.

At a ceremony in the north Jutland port of Frederikshavn, local shipbuilder Oerskov Christensen Skibsvaerft A/S, Russian fishing group JSC Sevryba and seafood group Royal Greenland A/S signed a pact to share knowhow and help modernise the north Russian fishing fleet.

"This is only part of a programme to renew our fleet, other steps will follow. I expect this to be a highly successful project and bankers and investors should have no doubts that they will get their money back with interest," JSC Sevryba managing director Georgy Tishkov told a news conference held to announce the deal.

The backbone of the project is a new Cyprus-registered company, Sevryba International Ltd to be owned by the three main partners with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Investment Fund for Eastern Europe, Denmark's Ship Credit Fund and other Danish investors.

The new partnership said it could not immediately give a breakdown of the ownership structure as some investors had yet to receive formal approval from their full boards, but the company would have share capital of 200 million Danish crowns ($34.42 million).

Oerskov Christensen is privately owned, Sevryba is owned 80 percent by north Russian fishing operators and 20 percent by the Russian government. Royal Greenland is fully owned by the government of Greenland, a self-governing Arctic province of Denmark.

The main terms of the deal are that Royal Greenland, one of the world's leading producers of fish and shellfish, will share its production and marketing experience with Sevryba through a joint management company, Royal Ryba A/S.

Oerskov Christensen, the Danish shipbuilder, will build four modern factory ships, at a cost of around 500 million crowns, which will be leased to Russian registered subsidiaries of Sevryba International until loans are repaid, in eight to nine years, and will then become their property.
Delivery is scheduled to commence by January 1998, with completion of the final vessel by October of the same year.

The shipbuilding element is a welcome fillip to Denmark's shipbulding industry, which has an annual turnover of around six billion crowns and has been hit by the strong crown and by foreign competitors subsidised by their governments.

Sevryba technical director Vladimir Khiznyakov said that ageing equipment and cumbersome administration inherited from the former Soviet system had been a barrier to the full exploitation of Russian fish quotas but the industry was now adapting to new market conditions.
"We must make a new economical, profitable industry, this is the only way for us because if we do not change, we have no future," he told Reuters.
The Russian partner currently produces 750,000 tonnes of fish annually, 50 percent of which is cod and haddock, and supplies about 25 percent of the Russian market, he said.
He did not say by how much he expected the new alliance to raise production.

Greenland fisheries minister Paaviaaraq Heilmann said that the pact would not generate enough income to significantly dent his country's economic dependence on Denmark, which contributes about 60 per cent of the home rule government's revenue.

But he said that the deal allowed for some of the joint venture's resources to be switched back to Greenland should cod stocks, which have almost vanished over the past 30 years due to a rise in sea temperature, return.
"If the cod come to Greenland and there are no other available trawlers, there will be a place for these vessels in helping us fulfil our quota," he said.
